# TypeScript types

Piral is fully typed around a single type: **`PiletApi`**, the contract a pilet uses to talk to the shell. This guide covers where that type comes from, how to extend it for your own events and extension slots, and how to share types across teams.

## How the types are generated

You don't hand-write the `PiletApi` type. When you build the app shell, Piral **generates** it:

```bash
npx piral build
```

The emulator produced by the build contains a generated TypeScript declaration (an `index.d.ts`) describing *that shell's* `PiletApi` — the [core API](/concepts/pilet-api#core-api) plus the methods of every plugin the shell installed. (The `piral declaration` command produces it; the build runs it for you.)

A pilet installs that emulator and imports the type:

```tsx
import type { PiletApi } from 'my-app-shell';

export function setup(api: PiletApi) {
  api.showNotification('Hi'); // ✅ typed only if the shell installed piral-notifications
}
```

Because the type is generated from the real shell, a pilet's autocomplete matches production exactly: call a method the shell doesn't provide and it's a compile error, not a runtime surprise. For framework-agnostic utilities that should accept any shell's API, import the base type instead:

```tsx
import type { PiletApi } from 'piral-core';
```

## Extending the types

Piral exposes a set of intentionally empty interfaces in `piral-core/lib/types/custom`. You extend the typing by **declaration merging** against them. Put these augmentations in a `.d.ts` file in the **app shell** so they flow into the generated emulator types (or in a shared types package — see below).

### Typing events

Augment `PiralCustomEventMap` so `api.emit` and `api.on` are checked:

```ts
// types.d.ts (in the app shell)
import 'piral-core';

declare module 'piral-core/lib/types/custom' {
  interface PiralCustomEventMap {
    'cart-item-added': { productId: string; quantity: number };
  }
}
```

```ts
api.emit('cart-item-added', { productId: 'p1', quantity: 2 }); // ✅ payload checked
api.on('cart-item-added', ({ productId, quantity }) => {
  // productId: string, quantity: number — fully typed
});
```

### Typing extension slots

Augment `PiralCustomExtensionSlotMap` to map each slot name to the shape of its `params`:

```ts
declare module 'piral-core/lib/types/custom' {
  interface PiralCustomExtensionSlotMap {
    'cart-extra': { cartTotal: number };
  }
}
```

Now both ends of the slot are type-checked:

```tsx
// rendering the slot
<ExtensionSlot name="cart-extra" params={{ cartTotal: 89.9 }} />

// filling the slot
api.registerExtension('cart-extra', ({ params }) => (
  <Promo total={params.cartTotal} /> // params is typed
));
```

### Other extension points

The same module exposes interfaces for more of the surface — for example `PiletCustomApi` to add methods to the Pilet API itself (this is what plugin authors merge into; see [Piral Plugins](/api/piral-plugin)), plus interfaces for shared data, page metadata, and custom errors. Augment whichever one you need; the pattern is always the same.

## Sharing types

Two pilets that emit the same event or fill the same slot need the *same* augmentations. Define the contract once and reuse it:

- **A shared types package.** Extract the `declare module` augmentations into a small package (e.g. `@my-portal/types`) that the shell and every pilet reference. The contract lives in one place.
- **Automatic fusion via Piral Cloud.** The official [Piral Cloud](https://www.piral.cloud) feed service can go a step further: pilets publish their own types, and the feed **automatically fuses the types published from pilets** into the instance's typing. Consumers then get a complete, always-current typed surface — including types contributed by other teams' pilets — without manually wiring up a shared package.

:::tip
Keep event and slot augmentations close to whoever *owns* the contract. If the app shell defines a slot, type it in the shell so the definition travels with the generated emulator types. If a pilet introduces a cross-pilet event, a shared types package (or Piral Cloud's type fusion) keeps every consumer in sync.
:::

Source: /guides/deployment

# Deploying to production

A Piral application has **two independent deployment streams**, and keeping them separate is the whole point:

- The **app shell** is a static site. You build it once and host the `dist/release/` output like any SPA. It changes rarely.
- **Pilets** are published to a **feed service**, not bundled into the shell. They ship continuously, on each team's own schedule, without ever redeploying the shell.

This page covers both, plus the server configuration and caching that make it reliable.

_(Diagram: Two independent pipelines: the shell deploys as a static site, pilets publish to the feed — and they meet only in the browser.)_

## Deploying the app shell

`npm run build` produces `dist/release/` — plain static files (HTML, JS, CSS, assets). Serve them from any static host or web server. There is one hard requirement: because routing is client-side, the server must **fall back to `index.html`** for any path that isn't a real file, so deep links and refreshes work.

### Self-hosted: nginx

A complete server block for a self-hosted static deployment, with SPA fallback, compression, and correct caching:

```nginx
server {
  listen 443 ssl http2;
  server_name app.example.com;
  root /var/www/my-portal;          # contents of dist/release/
  index index.html;

  gzip on;
  gzip_types text/css application/javascript application/json image/svg+xml;
  gzip_min_length 1024;

  # Hashed assets never change — cache them aggressively
  location /assets/ {
    expires 1y;
    add_header Cache-Control "public, immutable";
    try_files $uri =404;
  }

  # The HTML entry point must never be cached
  location = /index.html {
    add_header Cache-Control "no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate";
  }

  # SPA fallback: every other route renders the app shell
  location / {
    try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;
  }
}
```

### Self-hosted: Apache / IIS

For Apache, an `.htaccess` in the web root handles the fallback:

```apache
<IfModule mod_rewrite.c>
  RewriteEngine On
  RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-f
  RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d
  RewriteRule . /index.html [L]
</IfModule>
```

For IIS, add a rewrite rule in `web.config` that maps non-file requests to `/index.html`. The principle is identical: real files are served as-is, everything else returns the shell.

### Managed static hosts

Most platforms need only a one-line fallback rule:

| Host | SPA fallback configuration |
|---|---|
| Netlify | `_redirects`: `/* /index.html 200` |
| Vercel | `vercel.json` rewrite: `"source": "/(.*)", "destination": "/index.html"` |
| GitHub Pages | Copy `index.html` to `404.html` |
| Azure Static Web Apps | `staticwebapp.config.json` `navigationFallback` → `/index.html` |
| AWS S3 + CloudFront | Set the error document to `index.html` (403/404 → 200) |

### App shell via GitHub Actions

```yaml
name: Deploy app shell
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: write
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20 }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run build
      - uses: peaceiris/actions-gh-pages@v4
        with:
          github_token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          publish_dir: ./dist/release
```

### App shell to AWS S3 + CloudFront

```bash
aws s3 sync dist/release s3://my-bucket --delete
aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id $CF_DIST_ID --paths "/*"
```

## Caching strategy

Get these headers right and the app feels instant while still updating predictably:

```
# Hashed asset bundles (app shell + pilets) — cache forever
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# index.html — never cache, so new releases are picked up immediately
Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate

# The feed response — short TTL so rollouts/rollbacks propagate fast
Cache-Control: public, max-age=30, stale-while-revalidate=60
```

The feed TTL is the lever that controls how quickly a pilet rollout or rollback reaches users — typically within 30–60 seconds.

## Deploying pilets

Pilets never go through the app shell's pipeline. Each pilet builds and publishes to the feed independently:

```yaml
name: Publish pilet
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20 }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
      - run: npx pilet build
      - run: npx pilet publish --url ${{ vars.FEED_URL }}/api/v1/pilets --api-key ${{ secrets.FEED_API_KEY }}
```

The feed stores the bundle on your CDN and records the new version; the next feed response includes it. Where the feed lives — [Piral Cloud](https://www.piral.cloud) or a [custom feed service](/advanced/custom-feed) — doesn't change the publish step.

## Rollback

Because the shell only knows the feed URL, rolling back a pilet never touches the shell. Point the feed at the previous version and users pick it up on their next load:

| Feed type | How to roll back |
|---|---|
| Piral Cloud | One click in the dashboard |
| Self-hosted feed | Set the active version in your database |
| Static JSON feed | Edit the `version` / `link` in the JSON file |

No app shell rebuild, no `git revert`, no redeploy.

Source: /guides/llms
========================================================================

# Using LLMs with Piral

AI coding assistants — Copilot, Cursor, Claude, and friends — pair unusually well with Piral. A micro frontend is already split into small, self-contained units, so a pilet is a bite-sized, low-blast-radius task a model can reason about from end to end. This guide covers how to get good results, and how to make your own Piral app easy for assistants to work with.

## Why Piral fits LLM-assisted development

- **Small units.** A pilet is one feature behind one `setup(api)` function — small enough to hold in context and reason about completely.
- **A typed contract.** The Pilet API is fully typed. Point the model at the type and it knows exactly which registrations and methods exist, instead of guessing.
- **Isolation.** A wrong suggestion inside one pilet can't break the app shell or another pilet, so it's safe to let a model iterate.
- **Explicit boundaries.** Shared dependencies (importmaps) and extension slot names are written down — concrete facts a model can respect rather than infer.

## Give the model the right context

Context is the single biggest quality lever. Before asking for code, make sure the assistant has:

1. **The docs index.** Point your tool at this site's machine-readable `/llms.txt` — a curated map of every page so the model can pull the right reference on demand.
2. **The `PiletApi` type.** Paste (or reference) the `PiletApi` type from your app shell package — the emulator ships these definitions. This is the highest-value piece of context: it tells the model precisely which methods exist, so it won't invent `api.showNotification` when you haven't installed `piral-notifications`.
3. **The target shell and shared dependencies.** Name the app shell package and list the centrally shared externals (from the shell's importmap), so generated code treats `react` and friends as provided rather than bundling them.
4. **Slot names and config.** The extension slot names and their `params`, plus any feed `config` keys the pilet should read.

A short preamble like this, pasted into the chat or kept in a rules file, dramatically improves output:

```text
We build on Piral (React micro frontends).
Target app shell: my-app-shell  (import types via: import type { PiletApi } from 'my-app-shell').
Installed plugins (only these API methods exist): piral-menu, piral-notifications.
Shared externals (never bundle): react, react-dom, react-router-dom.
Extension slots: cart-extra (params: { cartTotal: number }).
Scaffold with `npm init pilet`; never install piral-cli globally.
```

## Common tasks

Each of these is a natural, well-scoped request for an assistant. The notes call out where models trained on older material tend to slip.

**Scaffold a pilet.** Ask for the current initializer, not the legacy command:

```bash
npm init pilet@latest -- --source my-app-shell --target my-pilet --bundler webpack5
```

If the model suggests `pilet new` or a global `npm i -g piral-cli`, that's stale — correct it (see [CLI reference](/reference/cli)).

**Register a page and a menu item.** A pilet exports exactly one `setup` function:

```tsx
import type { PiletApi } from 'my-app-shell';

export function setup(api: PiletApi) {
  api.registerPage('/orders', OrdersPage);
  api.registerMenu(() => <a href="/orders">Orders</a>);
}
```

**Fill an extension slot.** Remind the model that pilets never import each other — they connect through named slots (see [Extension slots](/concepts/extension-slots)).

**Share a library.** Ask it to add the package to the pilet's `importmap` rather than bundling it (see [Dependency sharing](/concepts/dependency-sharing)).

**Write tests.** "Write Vitest tests for this pilet's `setup` using a mock `PiletApi`" works well, because the registration logic is plain and framework-independent (see [Testing pilets](/guides/testing)).

**Migrate `piral` to `piral-core`.** Point the model at the [Piral packages](/reference/piral-packages) guide — the change is mechanical (swap the dependency, move plugin imports, register plugins explicitly).

## Guardrails to give the model

Models often carry outdated Piral habits from their training data. Stating these rules up front prevents the most common mistakes:

- Scaffold with `npm init piral-instance` / `npm init pilet`; run the CLI via `npx` or npm scripts. Never `npm i -g piral-cli`, never `piral new` / `pilet new`.
- A pilet's only required entry is an exported `setup(api)` function.
- Only call Pilet API methods provided by installed plugins; import `PiletApi` from the shell package for accurate, type-checked autocomplete.
- Treat `react`, `react-dom`, the router, and other shared libraries as externals via the importmap — don't bundle them or import a different version.
- Pilets never import one another: compose UI through extension slots, and share data through events, the shared data store, or a shared library.
- Registrations are cleaned up automatically on unload and hot reload; only call `unregister*` for genuinely dynamic cases.

## A drop-in rules file

Most assistants read a project-level instructions file — `AGENTS.md`, `.cursorrules`, or `.github/copilot-instructions.md`. Dropping one into your repo makes every tool follow your conventions automatically. Use this as a starting point and fill in your shell name, plugins, externals, and slots:

```text
# Piral project rules (for AI assistants)

This repository uses Piral (React micro frontends).

Contract:
- App shell package: my-app-shell. Types: import type { PiletApi } from 'my-app-shell'.
- Installed Pilet API plugins (only these methods exist): piral-menu, piral-notifications, piral-modals.
- Shared externals (never bundle, never import a different version): react, react-dom, react-router-dom.
- Extension slots: cart-extra (params: { cartTotal: number }).

Conventions:
- Scaffold with: npm init pilet@latest -- --source my-app-shell
- Never install piral-cli globally; never use `pilet new` or `piral new`.
- Run the CLI via npm scripts or npx (npx pilet debug | build | publish).
- A pilet's entry is a single exported setup(api: PiletApi) function.
- Only call Pilet API methods provided by the plugins listed above. Do not invent methods.
- Share libraries via the importmap in package.json; the externals above come from the shell.
- Pilets must not import each other. Compose UI via extension slots; share data via events or the shared data store.
- Prefer piral-core for long-lived apps (same API as piral).
- Write tests with Vitest by unit-testing setup() with a mock PiletApi.

Docs: see /llms.txt for a machine-readable map of the framework documentation.
```

## Make your app shell LLM-friendly

If you maintain the app shell, a little effort makes every pilet team's assistant far more accurate:

- **Ship accurate types.** The emulator already exports `PiletApi`; keep it in sync with the plugins you actually install so the model's view matches reality.
- **Document the contract.** List installed plugins, centrally shared dependencies, extension slot names and `params`, and feed `config` keys in one discoverable place.
- **Provide a template rules file.** Include a pre-filled `AGENTS.md` (like the one above) in your pilet scaffolding template so new pilets start LLM-ready.
- **Expose an `llms.txt`.** If you host your own developer portal or docs, add an `llms.txt` index — this site ships one at `/llms.txt` — so assistants can navigate it.

:::tip
The properties that make Piral good for teams make it good for assistants too: small, typed, isolated units with explicit contracts. The clearer your contracts, the better both humans and models perform.
:::

## Ready-made LLM assets

This documentation ships three assets you can point tools at or copy into your project:

- `/llms.txt` — a curated, linked index of every page (the [llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org) convention).
- `/llms-full.txt` — the entire documentation concatenated as plain text, regenerated on every build; ideal for pasting into a model's context or ingesting wholesale.
- `/AGENTS.md` — a ready-to-edit version of the rules file above. Download it, fill in your shell name, plugins, externals, and slots, then drop it into your repo as `AGENTS.md` (or `.cursorrules` / `.github/copilot-instructions.md`).

If you maintain a custom pilet scaffolding template, include a pre-filled `AGENTS.md` so every new pilet starts LLM-ready — a custom template is the natural place to ship conventions like this.


========================================================================
Source: /advanced/custom-feed
========================================================================

# Custom feed services

The feed service is Piral's discovery layer: on startup the app shell asks it which pilets to load, and `pilet publish` sends new versions to it. Most teams use the managed [Piral Cloud](https://www.piral.cloud) feed and never build one — but the protocol is deliberately small, so running your own is very doable when you need full control, custom targeting logic, or on-prem hosting. This page walks through a minimal, production-shaped implementation you can grow from.

## The protocol

A feed is just two HTTP endpoints — one the shell reads on startup, one the CLI writes to when publishing. Everything else (storage, targeting, rollback) is your implementation detail.

Two endpoints required:

```
GET  /api/v1/pilets          ← called by the app shell on startup
POST /api/v1/pilets          ← called by `npx pilet publish`
```

## Minimal Node.js implementation

The read endpoint returns the metadata the shell needs for each pilet — name, version, bundle URL, and integrity hash. Because it sees the request, it's also where per-user logic lives: filter by role, tenant, or cohort so different users get different pilet sets. The publish endpoint accepts the packed pilet, stores the bundle on a CDN, and records the new version in a database:

```ts
import express from 'express';
import multer from 'multer';

const app = express();
const upload = multer({ storage: multer.memoryStorage() });

app.get('/api/v1/pilets', async (req, res) => {
  const user = await verifyToken(req.headers.authorization);
  const all = await db.getActivePilets();

  const visible = all.filter(p =>
    (!p.requiredRole || user.roles.includes(p.requiredRole)) &&
    (!p.tenantId || p.tenantId === user.tenantId)
  );

  res.json({
    items: visible.map(p => ({
      name: p.name,
      version: p.version,
      link: `${CDN_BASE}/${p.name}@${p.version}/index.js`,
      spec: 'v2',
      integrity: p.integrity,
      dependencies: {},
      config: p.config ?? {},
    })),
  });
});

app.post('/api/v1/pilets', verifyApiKey, upload.single('file'), async (req, res) => {
  const meta = await extractPiletMeta(req.file.buffer);
  await uploadToCDN(`${meta.name}@${meta.version}/index.js`, req.file.buffer);
  await db.upsertPilet({ name: meta.name, version: meta.version });
  res.json({ name: meta.name, version: meta.version });
});

app.listen(9000);
```

## Database schema (PostgreSQL)

```sql
CREATE TABLE pilets (
  id           SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name         TEXT NOT NULL,
  version      TEXT NOT NULL,
  integrity    TEXT,
  config       JSONB DEFAULT '{}',
  active       BOOLEAN DEFAULT true,
  published_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE(name, version)
);
```

## Rollback endpoint

```ts
app.patch('/api/admin/pilets/:name/rollback', adminOnly, async (req, res) => {
  const { name } = req.params;
  const { version } = req.body;
  await db.query(
    'UPDATE pilets SET active = (version = $2) WHERE name = $1',
    [name, version]
  );
  res.json({ name, activeVersion: version });
});
```

## CDN storage

The feed only ever returns *URLs* to bundles — it doesn't serve the JavaScript itself. Host the bundles as static, content-addressed files (each at a `name@version` path) so they can be cached forever and never collide. Any HTTPS-capable static host works:

Pilet bundles must be publicly accessible over HTTPS.

| Option | Notes |
|---|---|
| AWS S3 + CloudFront | Production standard. Set `Cache-Control: immutable`. |
| Azure Blob + CDN | Same pattern on Azure. |
| Cloudflare R2 | Zero egress cost. |
| GitHub Releases | Free, adequate for low-traffic internal tools. |

## Feed caching

```
Cache-Control: public, max-age=30, stale-while-revalidate=60
```

30-second TTL means rollbacks propagate within 30–60 seconds. Adjust to taste.


========================================================================
Source: /advanced/performance
========================================================================

# Performance & lazy loading

## The default loading model

On startup, the app shell:

1. Fetches the feed (one request)
2. Loads every pilet's JS bundle in parallel
3. Calls each pilet's `setup()`

With 30 pilets averaging 80 KB gzipped, that's 2.4 MB before the page is interactive — even if the user only needs three pilets. The strategies below cut that down.

_(Diagram: Eager loading downloads every pilet up front; lazy techniques defer code until it's actually needed.)_

## Pilets are fast by default

Before reaching for any strategy, it's worth knowing that pilets are inherently fast:

- **Small entry, parallel streaming.** A pilet's `index.js` is small, so it loads quickly — and over HTTP/2 (and newer) many small files stream in parallel, so requesting several pilets at once isn't the penalty it was under HTTP/1.
- **Cached indefinitely, no collisions.** Each pilet is served from a path that contains its **name and version**, so versions can never collide and bundles can be cached **forever**. (The official [Piral Cloud](https://www.piral.cloud) feed serves them exactly this way.)
- **Warm loads beat an SPA.** Because unchanged pilets are already on disk from a previous visit, a returning user often loads *faster* than with an equivalent monolithic SPA — only the pilets that actually changed are fetched again.

So the strategies below matter mostly at larger scale (dozens of pilets) or to shave the very first paint — not as everyday necessities.

## Strategy 1: Code splitting within a pilet

This is the everyday lazy-loading technique, and it's always available. Split heavy pages with `React.lazy` so a pilet ships a small entry and pulls in the rest only when a route is opened:

```tsx
const DashboardPage = React.lazy(() => import('./pages/DashboardPage'));
const ReportsPage   = React.lazy(() => import('./pages/ReportsPage'));

export function setup(api: PiletApi) {
  api.registerPage('/analytics', DashboardPage);
  api.registerPage('/analytics/reports', ReportsPage);
}
```

Wrap the shell's `RouteSwitch` in `<Suspense>` so the chunk can load gracefully:

```tsx
const RouteSwitch: React.FC = ({ children }) => (
  <React.Suspense fallback={<PageSkeleton />}>
    {children}
  </React.Suspense>
);
```

The pilet still loads at startup, but it stays tiny; the bulk arrives on navigation. Reach for this first — it needs no shell coordination and no feed changes.

## Strategy 2: Deferring whole pilets from the app shell

Sometimes you want to keep an *entire* pilet out of the initial load — an admin area, a rarely used reporting module — without splitting it internally. Because **you** own `requestPilets`, the shell can decide which pilets load at startup and which load later. A nice side effect: this needs no feed-side orchestration — a static JSON file or a fixed list is enough, since the *shell* does the filtering and the timing.

```tsx
const all = await loadPiletList(); // a static JSON, a fixed list, or a feed response
const eager = all.filter((p) => !p.custom?.deferred);
const deferred = all.filter((p) => p.custom?.deferred);

const instance = createInstance({
  requestPilets: () => Promise.resolve(eager), // load only the essentials at startup
});

// …later, when the condition applies (a feature flag, a role, a route, a "load more"):
const meta = deferred.find((p) => p.name === 'pilet-reports');
await instance.context.addPilet(meta); // load + evaluate + inject on demand
```

`instance.context.addPilet(meta)` fetches, evaluates, and injects the pilet at runtime — its pages, menu items, and extensions light up immediately. The companion `removePilet(name)` tears one down again, and `injectPilet(pilet)` injects an already-loaded one.

Use Strategy 2 when the unit you want to defer is a whole pilet and the decision lives in the shell; use Strategy 1 when the deferral is *within* a single pilet.

## Strategy 3: Optimise shared dependencies

Audit what each pilet actually bundles:

```bash
npx pilet build --source-maps
npx source-map-explorer dist/index.js
```

If you see React, the router, or your design system inside multiple pilet bundles, move them to the app shell's `importmap` (central externals). For domain libraries shared between only some pilets, use a pilet-level `importmap` side-bundle instead. See [Dependency sharing](/concepts/dependency-sharing).

## Strategy 4: CDN caching

Pilet bundles have content-hashed filenames by default. Cache them forever:

```
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
```

Only `index.html` and the feed JSON should have short cache TTLs.

## Strategy 5: Eliminate the feed round trip

The one thing that can make a Piral app's *first* load longer than a plain SPA is the extra hop to the feed service: the shell loads, asks the feed which pilets to use, then loads them. You can remove that hop by serving `index.html` **dynamically** rather than statically — take the usual static `index.html` and augment it so it already carries the feed response.

Inline the pilet list into the document (for example as a small script the shell reads instead of fetching), and point `requestPilets` at it:

```html
<!-- injected by the server into index.html -->
<script>
  window.__pilets__ = [ /* the feed response, rendered server-side */ ];
</script>
```

```tsx
const instance = createInstance({
  requestPilets: () => Promise.resolve((window as any).__pilets__ ?? fetchFeed()),
});
```

Now the shell starts loading pilets immediately — there's no separate feed request. In the warm-load case those bundles are already cached on disk, so they're available at once, with no network round trip at all for unchanged pilets. This pairs naturally with a server-rendered shell; see [Server-side rendering](/advanced/ssr).

## Performance targets

| Artifact | Good | Warning |
|---|---|---|
| App shell JS (gzipped) | < 100 KB | > 200 KB |
| Individual pilet (gzipped) | < 60 KB | > 150 KB |
| Feed response JSON | < 5 KB | > 20 KB |
| Time to first pilet render | < 2s (fast connection) | > 4s |


========================================================================
Source: /advanced/module-federation
========================================================================

# Module & Native Federation

When people compare Piral to "federation," they usually mean one of two things: **Module Federation** or **Native Federation**. Both solve the *loading* layer of a micro frontend — getting code from one independently built app into another at runtime. Piral solves that layer too, but wraps a whole framework around it. This page draws the lines clearly and shows how they combine.

## What they all share

All three let you:

- Deploy UI modules independently of the host.
- Share dependencies (React, etc.) at runtime instead of bundling them everywhere.
- Load code dynamically, without one monolithic bundle.

The difference is how much of the system each one gives you out of the box.

## The three approaches

**Module Federation** is a code-sharing mechanism baked into a bundler. One build exposes modules; another consumes them at runtime. It originated in Webpack 5, and with **Module Federation 2.0** it's no longer Webpack-only — it runs on Rspack and has a bundler-independent runtime, with community plugins for Vite and others. What it still doesn't define for you: how to *discover* which remotes to load, how modules *register* themselves into the host, local developer experience, or the end-to-end CLI workflow.

**Native Federation** takes the same idea but builds it on web standards — native ES modules and [import maps](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/script/type/importmap) — instead of bundler internals. It's bundler-agnostic and framework-agnostic (it grew up in the Angular ecosystem but isn't tied to it), which makes it lightweight and future-proof. Like Module Federation, it's a transport layer: discovery, registration, and tooling are still yours to assemble.

**Piral** is a complete micro frontend *framework*. It includes the discovery layer (the feed service), a typed registration contract (the Pilet API), local development tooling (the emulator and CLI), and runtime UI composition (extension slots). Crucially, Piral is **not a competitor to the transports** — it can load pilets, Module Federation remotes, *and* Native Federation remotes, so the federation choice becomes an implementation detail underneath Piral.

```
Module Federation / Native Federation  →  the "how" (transport)
Piral                                  →  the "how" + "what" + "when" + tooling
```

## Feature comparison

| Capability | Module Federation | Native Federation | Piral |
|---|---|---|---|
| Transport for remote modules | ✅ bundler runtime | ✅ import maps + ESM | ✅ (+ can reuse the other two) |
| Bundler independence | ✅ since MF 2.0 | ✅ by design | ✅ (pick any bundler plugin) |
| Standards-based (no runtime lib) | ❌ | ✅ | ⚠️ uses a small runtime |
| Dynamic runtime discovery | ❌ DIY | ❌ DIY | ✅ feed service |
| Typed registration contract | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ Pilet API |
| Developer emulator | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ built-in |
| Extension / slot composition | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ built-in |
| Per-user / per-tenant targeting | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ via feed |
| Instant rollback without redeploy | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ via feed |
| End-to-end CLI workflow | ⚠️ partial | ⚠️ partial | ✅ full |

## When a transport alone is enough

Reach for Module Federation or Native Federation **without** Piral when:

- You only need to share code between a small, fixed set of apps you already control.
- You don't need runtime discovery, per-user targeting, or instant rollback.
- You want the absolute minimum runtime — in which case **Native Federation** is the most standards-aligned choice, and **Module Federation** is the natural fit if you're already invested in its ecosystem (e.g. Rspack or Next.js).

## When to choose Piral

- You want discovery, targeting, and rollback handled for you rather than built by hand.
- A stable, typed registration contract between host and modules matters.
- Developer experience — the emulator, CLI, and extension slots — is a priority.
- You have many independently deployed modules and multiple teams.

## Using them together

These are composable, not mutually exclusive. Piral can treat a Module Federation or Native Federation remote as a pilet: the feed describes the remote (a pilet with `spec: "mf"`, or a native-federation remote entry) and Piral loads it like any other pilet — while you keep the feed, emulator, typed API, and extension slots on top.

In other words, you don't have to pick "Piral *or* federation." You pick a federation transport for *how* code is delivered, and Piral for *everything around it*.


========================================================================
Source: /advanced/pilet-portability
========================================================================

# Pilet portability

When you scaffold a pilet with `--source my-app-shell`, it's easy to assume the pilet is *bound* to that shell. It isn't. That reference exists so the pilet can compile against the shell's TypeScript types and run inside its emulator during development. At **runtime**, a pilet is far more portable: any app shell that satisfies the pilet's assumptions can host it — including a *newer version* of the same shell, or an *entirely different* shell the pilet was never "developed for."

## What a pilet actually depends on

A pilet doesn't depend on a specific shell build. It depends on a set of **capabilities** being present at runtime:

1. **The Pilet API surface it calls.** If a pilet uses `api.registerPage` and `api.showNotification`, the host shell must provide those — meaning it must have the corresponding plugins installed (here, `piral-notifications`).
2. **The centrally shared dependencies it treats as externals.** A pilet that compiles `react` and `react-router-dom` as externals expects the host to provide them at runtime.
3. **Any cross-pilet contracts it relies on.** Extension slot names it fills, shared-data keys it reads, events it listens for.

If a host shell provides all of these, the pilet runs. If it's missing one — say, no notifications plugin — the pilet will fail where it tries to use the absent capability. That's the entire contract.

_(Diagram: The same pilet binary runs on any shell that satisfies its assumptions — not just the one it was scaffolded against.)_

## Why this matters

**You can upgrade the shell without rebuilding pilets.** As long as a new shell version keeps providing the API methods and shared dependencies existing pilets use, those pilets keep working untouched. This is how a single shell can host dozens of independently maintained pilets across many versions — old API methods remain present; new ones simply become available to pilets that upgrade their emulator. (See [Emulator → version coordination](/concepts/emulator#version-coordination).)

**You can reuse a pilet across shells.** A "profile" or "notifications" pilet can run in several different portals, as long as each portal's shell offers the capabilities the pilet relies on. The pilet is authored once and dropped into each shell's feed.

**The dev-time link is just a default, not a lock.** The `piral.name` field and the emulator dev dependency tell the tooling which shell to type-check and debug against. They don't restrict where the built pilet can run.

## Keeping pilets portable

- **Depend on the API, not the implementation.** Use the typed Pilet API and shared externals; avoid reaching into shell internals or `window` globals.
- **Treat the API as a versioned contract.** Additive changes keep old pilets working; removing or changing a method is a breaking change for every pilet that uses it.
- **Document the capabilities a shell must provide** — which plugins, which centrally shared packages, which extension slot names — so a pilet can be matched to any compatible shell with confidence.

:::tip The flip side
Portability cuts both ways: if a pilet quietly assumes a plugin or shared package that a target shell doesn't provide, it will break there. Make assumptions explicit (and ideally type-checked against the target emulator) rather than implicit.
:::


========================================================================
Source: /advanced/monorepo
========================================================================

# Monorepo setup

Pilets are built and deployed independently — but during development it's often convenient to keep the app shell and several pilets in one repository. You get shared tooling, atomic cross-cutting refactors, and instant local linking with no publish step. A workspace manager (pnpm, Yarn, or npm workspaces) plus a task runner is all it takes, and it changes nothing about how the pieces *deploy*: each pilet still ships on its own.

## Structure

```
my-portal/
├── packages/
│   ├── app-shell/
│   ├── pilet-checkout/
│   ├── pilet-catalog/
│   └── pilet-account/
├── package.json       ← workspace root
└── pnpm-workspace.yaml
```

## pnpm workspaces

`pnpm-workspace.yaml`:

```yaml
packages:
  - 'packages/*'
```

Root `package.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "my-portal-monorepo",
  "private": true,
  "scripts": {
    "dev:shell": "pnpm --filter app-shell dev",
    "build:all": "pnpm -r build",
    "test:all": "pnpm -r test"
  }
}
```

## Pilet references the local app shell

A pilet always targets a shell by name. In a monorepo that target resolves to the **sibling package** instead of a published one, so a pilet develops against the shell in the same repo:

In `packages/pilet-checkout/package.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "pilet-checkout",
  "devDependencies": {
    "app-shell": "workspace:*"
  },
  "piral": { "name": "app-shell" }
}
```

`workspace:*` tells pnpm to use the local version — no npm publish needed during development.

## Turborepo (recommended for large repos)

As the repository grows, a task runner like Turborepo pays off: it caches build outputs and runs tasks only for packages that actually changed — a real time-saver once you have a dozen pilets and a shell to build and test:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://turbo.build/schema.json",
  "tasks": {
    "build": { "dependsOn": ["^build"], "outputs": ["dist/**"] },
    "test": { "dependsOn": ["build"] },
    "dev": { "cache": false, "persistent": true }
  }
}
```

:::tip
On Turborepo 1.x this top-level key was called `pipeline`; it was renamed to `tasks` in Turborepo 2.0.
:::

```bash
turbo build                    # build everything in order
turbo build --filter=[HEAD^1]  # only changed packages
```

## CI: only build what changed

```yaml
- name: Build affected
  run: turbo build --filter=[HEAD^1]

- name: Test affected
  run: turbo test --filter=[HEAD^1]
```


========================================================================
Source: /advanced/ssr
========================================================================

# Server-side rendering

Server-side rendering is an area of active development for Piral. The honest summary up front: **first-class SSR is being addressed in Piral v2**. Today you can already get good results with a static shell plus client hydration, and the modular foundation Piral gives you is exactly what makes a richer SSR story tractable.

## Why Piral is well-positioned for SSR

A Piral application is already a composition of independent modules. That maps almost one-to-one onto the **islands architecture**: each pilet is a self-contained island that can be rendered on the server and hydrated independently on the client, without forcing the whole page through a single monolithic render.

That modular foundation is the hard part — and Piral already has it. Layering SSR on top is then about *where* and *when* each island renders, rather than re-architecting the app. This is why building on Piral pays off even before the full SSR story lands: the structure you adopt now is the structure SSR wants.

## What works today: static shell + client hydration

The pragmatic approach available right now is to pre-render the app shell's skeleton as static HTML and let pilets load and hydrate on the client as usual.

```html
<body>
  <div id="app">
    <header class="app-header">
      <a href="/">My Portal</a>
      <nav id="shell-nav"><!-- pilets fill this --></nav>
    </header>
    <main id="shell-main">
      <div class="loading-placeholder">Loading…</div>
    </main>
  </div>
  <script src="/app-shell.js" defer></script>
</body>
```

This gives you a fast, meaningful first paint (header, navigation, layout) with no server-side rendering infrastructure for the pilets themselves. The trade-off is that pilet content isn't in the initial HTML, so it's not ideal for SEO on pilet-rendered pages. For many internal tools and authenticated apps, that's a perfectly good place to stand.

## The direction: islands SSR in Piral v2

The cohesive, first-class SSR story is landing in **Piral v2**, built around the islands model described above — server-rendering pilets and hydrating them independently.

You can already see the direction in an early prototype: the [Netflix islands demo](https://github.com/piral-samples/netflix-islands-demo) is a Netflix-style portal whose pilets use the islands architecture (built on `piral-server`). It's an older, experimental sample rather than a supported API, but it shows where Piral is heading and what islands-based SSR looks like in practice.

:::tip
Adopt Piral now for the modularity, dynamism, and team independence it gives you today. The investment carries forward: when first-class SSR arrives in v2, it builds on the same modular foundation rather than asking you to restructure.
:::

## Things to keep in mind

Regardless of the approach, a few constraints apply to any SSR setup:

- Pilets that touch browser-only APIs (`window`, `document`) need guards like `if (typeof window !== 'undefined')` so they can run (or no-op) on the server.
- Highly dynamic, per-user feeds make full-page output hard to cache — an argument for island-level rendering and hydration rather than monolithic SSR.
- Non-React pilets (via converters) depend on their framework's own SSR support.

If SEO on pilet-rendered content is a hard requirement today, start with the static shell approach and follow Piral v2 for the first-class path.


========================================================================
Source: /advanced/migration
========================================================================

# Migrating from a monolith

The strangler fig pattern: introduce Piral alongside your existing app, gradually expand it until the monolith can be retired.

## The migration stages

_(Diagram: The legacy app enters as a single pilet and is strangled feature-by-feature until only independent pilets remain.)_

## Step 1: Create a thin app shell

```bash
npm init piral-instance@latest -- --target my-portal --bundler webpack5
```

Add your existing global layout and auth mechanism. Leave the feed empty for now.

## Step 2: Wrap the existing app as a pilet

```tsx
// pilet-legacy/src/index.tsx
import type { PiletApi } from 'my-portal';

// Import your existing React app root component
// Remove the top-level <BrowserRouter> — Piral provides it
import { LegacyApp } from '../existing-app/src/LegacyApp';

export function setup(api: PiletApi) {
  // Catch-all: the legacy app handles all routes internally
  api.registerPage('/*', LegacyApp);
}
```

Remove the top-level `<BrowserRouter>` from `LegacyApp` — Piral's shell provides routing. Keep any internal `<Routes>` for nested navigation.

## Step 3: Validate

Build and publish the legacy pilet. Verify the full existing application works through the new shell. Fix CSS scoping issues if global styles conflict.

## Step 4: Extract features team by team

1. Create a new pilet for a feature (`pilet-checkout`)
2. Move the feature's components into it
3. Register the feature's routes in the new pilet
4. Remove those routes from the legacy pilet
5. Both teams now deploy independently

Repeat for each feature at each team's own pace.

## Step 5: Retire the legacy pilet

Once all features are extracted, disable the legacy pilet in the feed.

## Handling CSS

Scope all legacy global styles to avoid conflicts:

```tsx
const LegacyApp = () => (
  <div className="legacy-app-scope">
    <ActualLegacyApp />
  </div>
);
```

```css
.legacy-app-scope .button { /* scoped legacy styles */ }
```

## Timeline expectations

| App size | Teams | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| Small (< 20 routes) | 1–2 | 4–8 weeks |
| Medium (20–80 routes) | 3–6 | 3–6 months |
| Large (80+ routes) | 7+ | 9–18 months |

The upfront investment (stages 1–3) typically takes 1–3 weeks regardless of app size.


========================================================================
Source: /reference/cli
========================================================================

# CLI reference

Piral's tooling lives in the `piral-cli` package. You **don't install it globally**. Instead:

- **Scaffolding** is done with npm initializers (`npm init piral-instance`, `npm init pilet`), which download a throwaway scaffolder on demand.
- The initializers add `piral-cli` (plus a bundler plugin) as a **local dev dependency** of the generated project.
- You then run commands through the generated **npm scripts** (`npm start`, `npm run build`) or directly with **`npx`** (`npx pilet build`).

This keeps each project pinned to its own CLI and bundler versions, with nothing to maintain on your machine globally.

## Scaffolding

### `npm init piral-instance`

Create a new app shell.

```bash
npm init piral-instance@latest -- --target my-portal --bundler webpack5
```

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--target` | `.` | Output directory |
| `--bundler` | `webpack5` | `webpack5`, `esbuild`, `rspack`, `vite`, `parcel2` |
| `--npm-client` | `npm` | `npm`, `yarn`, `pnpm` |
| `--no-install` | — | Skip dependency installation |
| `--defaults` | — | Accept all defaults non-interactively |

### `npm init pilet`

Create a new pilet for a given app shell.

```bash
npm init pilet@latest -- --source my-portal --target my-feature-pilet --bundler webpack5
```

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--source` | — | App shell package name, or a path to its emulator `.tgz` |
| `--target` | `.` | Output directory |
| `--bundler` | `webpack5` | Bundler plugin to use |
| `--npm-client` | `npm` | `npm`, `yarn`, `pnpm` |

Everything after the `--` is forwarded to the initializer — don't drop it.

## App shell commands

Run these from inside a shell project, via the generated scripts or `npx`.

### `piral debug`

Start the app shell dev server (this is what `npm start` runs).

```bash
npx piral debug
```

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--port` | `1234` | Dev server port |
| `--open` | `false` | Open the browser on start |
| `--log-level` | `info` | `error`, `warn`, `info`, `verbose` |

### `piral build`

Build the app shell for production (this is what `npm run build` runs).

```bash
npx piral build
```

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--type` | `all` | `all`, `release`, `emulator` |
| `--target` | `./dist` | Output directory |
| `--minify` | `true` | Minify the release output |

The default `all` produces both `dist/release/` (deploy this) and `dist/emulator/` (publish this for pilet developers).

### `piral publish`

Publish the emulator package so pilet teams can install it.

```bash
npx piral publish --type emulator
```

This is equivalent to `npm publish dist/emulator/<shell>-<version>.tgz`. Use `--registry` to target a private registry.

## Pilet commands

Run these from inside a pilet project.

### `pilet debug`

Start the pilet dev server inside the emulated shell (this is what `npm start` runs). The target shell is read from your `package.json`.

```bash
npx pilet debug
npx pilet debug --feed https://feed.example.com/api/v1/pilets   # load extra pilets too
```

### `pilet build`

Build the pilet bundle.

```bash
npx pilet build
```

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--target` | `./dist` | Output directory |
| `--minify` | `true` | Minify the bundle |
| `--schema` | `v2` | Pilet spec: `v0`, `v1`, `v2`, `mf` |

### `pilet publish`

Build (if needed) and publish to a feed service. Choose how you authenticate:

```bash
# Locally / with a browser — log in interactively, no secret to handle
npx pilet publish --url https://feed.example.com/api/v1/pilets --interactive

# CI/CD / automation — use an API key from a secret
npx pilet publish --url https://feed.example.com/api/v1/pilets --api-key $FEED_API_KEY
```

| Option | Description |
|---|---|
| `--url` | Feed service publish endpoint (required) |
| `--interactive` | Log in via the browser instead of passing a key — preferred when you have a browser, since no secret is entered in the terminal |
| `--api-key` | API key for the feed — use this for CI/CD and other automation |
| `--from` | `pilet` (build first) or `file` (use an existing `.tgz`) |

:::tip Which auth flow?
Use `--interactive` for day-to-day publishing from a developer machine — you don't need to create or store a secret. Use `--api-key` (from a CI secret) for pipelines and any non-interactive automation.
:::

### `pilet upgrade`

Upgrade the emulator dev dependency to a newer shell version.

```bash
npx pilet upgrade          # latest
npx pilet upgrade 2.0.0    # pin to a version
```

### `pilet validate`

Check the pilet's format and metadata before publishing.

```bash
npx pilet validate
```

:::tip Add commands to your scripts
Generated projects already wire `npm start` and `npm run build` to the right CLI calls. Add the rest (`"publish": "pilet publish"`, `"validate": "pilet validate"`) to `package.json` so your team and CI use one consistent entry point.
:::
